name: The Hungarian Oak of Park Zijpendaal
access: Free, public landscape park and estate (Park Zijpendaal, freely accessible, open every day of the week per the park's own visitor information).
transport: About 20 minutes' walk from Arnhem Centraal station.
verify_notes: Register (LRMB nr 1692980) states this is the tallest measured Hungarian oak in the Netherlands, and so far in Europe. Planted 1900-1910, gemeente-owned, visitable=ja, visible=ja. History note from the register: it used to stand hemmed in on the west side by tall beeches, hence its crooked eastward lean; now standing more freely and showing recovery growth on the west side of the crown. SINGLE SOURCE for the species/age/superlative claim (the register itself); I could not independently confirm the 'tallest in NL/Europe' claim on a live page (monumentaltrees.com 403s automated fetches, and a WebSearch AI summary mentioning this is not treated as evidence per the search-summary rule). What IS independently confirmed via Wikipedia and Visit Arnhem: Park Zijpendaal is a genuine public landscape park, freely accessible, open daily, located north of Park Sonsbeek, which supports the access side of the verification even though the tree-specific facts rest on the register alone. Flag for the writer: state the register's own superlative claim as the register's claim, do not present it as independently verified. This tree extends the existing Zijpendaal pocket (arn_026, arn_027) into a second walk alongside Gulden Bodem.

name: The Twin Giant Sequoias of Gulden Bodem

location.address: Gulden Bodem, near the car park, Arnhem

access: Free, public park; Gulden Bodem is owned by the municipality of Arnhem and has been a national heritage site (rijksmonument) since 2006. Wikipedia's infobox lists it as 'open voor publiek'.
transport: About 23 minutes' walk from Arnhem Centraal station.
verify_notes: Register (LRMB nr 1692429) records TWO giant sequoias together at one point (n_trees=2) at Gulden Bodem, a former hunting-lodge estate now a public gemeente-owned park and rijksmonument since 2006. Register's own history text: 'goed zichtbaar vanaf de weg' (clearly visible from the road/path), planting year probably around 1870 when a now-vanished hunting lodge and coach house stood here with a landscape-style park around them; described as impressive trees in reasonable condition. This is a paired ensemble like the already-published De Poortwachters (arn_001, two sweet chestnuts at the same park) rather than a single specimen, so it ships as ONE entry describing both trees standing together, per the compact-ensemble allowance. SINGLE SOURCE for the trees themselves (the register); Wikipedia's Gulden Bodem article confirms the park is real, public and a rijksmonument, and separately names the chestnut 'Poortwachters' (as three trees 1650-1700, slightly at odds with the register's 'twee... 1700-1750' language for that already-published pair, a discrepancy for a future pass to note, not something this pass touches), but does not itself mention the sequoias. Flag accordingly. Not to be confused with the separately-registered Beukenrij Gulden Bodem (nr 1692428, a row of 7 beeches on an earthen bank), which is an avenue/stand and stays blocked as a non-collectible ensemble.

access: Free. Stands in front of the former St Elisabeth's Gasthuis building on Utrechtseweg, a public street; the complex itself is now apartments and a dental practice, both protected national monuments, but the register marks the tree itself visitable=ja, visible=ja, in front of (rather than behind or within) the building.

verify_notes: Register (LRMB nr 1678328) places this beech 'voor voormalig St. Elisabeth Gasthuis, Utrechtseweg' (in front of the former hospital, on Utrechtseweg), planted 1890-1900, owner_category 'publiekrechtelijke organisatie' (a public-law body, plausibly the housing/care institution that succeeded the hospital), visitable=ja, visible=ja. History field 'onbekend'. The building itself is independently confirmed via rijksmonumenten.nl and the national monument register (monumentenregister.cultureelerfgoed.nl) as a protected complex, now converted to apartments (St. Elisabethshof) with a dental practice; this corroborates the SITE and its street frontage on Utrechtseweg but not the tree's own species/age, which rests on the register alone. Flag accordingly. The 'in front of' phrasing plus visible=ja suggests street-side standing rather than an enclosed courtyard, consistent with hard rule 10's public-street reading, but a future pass should sanity-check via street-view or an OSM access-tag pass before this ships with full confidence.

name: The Cedar of Lebanon of Angerenstein
access: Free, public park. transport: About 8 minutes' walk from Arnhem Presikhaaf station (the nearest bus stop is on Rosendaalseweg).
verify_notes: Register (LRMB nr 1677478) is the oldest single tree found in this pass's two clusters: planted 1750-1800, gemeente-owned, setting 'park', visitable=ja. History field 'onbekend', so no register narrative beyond the planting band. Wikipedia and buitenplaatseninnederland.nl both independently confirm Park Angerenstein itself is a genuine 250-year-old estate, publicly owned since 1941 and open as a public park since 1921, with 'monumental trees' described generally, which supports the plausibility and access of this candidate without independently confirming this specific cedar's species or age. SINGLE SOURCE for the tree's own facts. Part of a tight, walkable four-tree pocket at Angerenstein alongside arn_035, arn_036 and arn_037, all within about 100m of each other and all gemeente-owned per the register, which settles the private-vs-public estate question the brief asked to check carefully: Angerenstein is NOT private, it has been a municipal public park since 1941.

name: The Tulip Tree of Angerenstein

location.address: In the park in front of Huis Angerenstein, Arnhem

access: Free, public park. Park Angerenstein has been municipally owned and open to the public since 1941; confirmed independently via Wikipedia and buitenplaatseninnederland.nl as a genuine, freely accessible public park.
transport: About 8 minutes' walk from Arnhem Presikhaaf station.
verify_notes: TWO INDEPENDENT SOURCES, this is the strongest candidate of the whole pass. Register (LRMB nr 1677479) places it 'in het park voor het huis Angerenstein' (in the park in front of the Angerenstein house), planted 1810-1820, gemeente-owned, visitable=ja. Independently, the local neighbourhood-history site angerenstein-arnhem.nl ('De grootste van Nederland', published 13 Feb 2011) measured it in December 2010 at 37.5 metres tall with a circumference of 5.39 metres at 1.3m height, described as one of the largest tulip trees in the Netherlands and possibly the fourth-thickest in Europe, growing about 3cm thicker in the year before that measurement, and estimated at roughly 200 years old at the time (so roughly 216 years old in 2026, consistent with the register's 1810-1820 planting band). This is a genuinely remarkable specimen: a 37.5m tulip tree is exceptional for the species in the Netherlands. Girth recorded as 539cm (converted from the 5.39m circumference figure). Good candidate to lead the Angerenstein write-up.
